name: Grandmillennial

influenced_by: traditional English and American chintz-and-antique interior decorating

media.title: House Beautiful's 2019 trend coverage
media.note: widely credited as an early vehicle for naming the trend

reacts_against: the flat, neutral, Instagram-friendly "millennial grey" interior style that had dominated home-decor media through the 2010s, reclaiming chintz, florals and inherited or secondhand antiques instead.
article: Grandmillennial decorating names a specific, well-documented reaction: interior-design media began using the term around 2019 to describe millennials furnishing homes with traditionally "grandmotherly" items — chintz floral fabric, needlepoint pillows, antique brass, scalloped trim — sourced largely from estate sales and secondhand shops, explicitly positioned against the flat grey, white and blush "millennial" minimalism that had dominated Instagram-era home decor through most of the 2010s. The trend carries a generational irony in its own name (millennials decorating like their grandmothers) that coverage of it consistently calls out, and it's closely tied to a broader early-2020s turn toward maximalism and inherited, storied objects over the clean, replaceable, flat-pack aesthetic that preceded it. Because the trend was named and tracked by design journalists in close to real time, its origin point is unusually easy to date compared to most interior-design movements, which tend to be identified only in retrospect.

findings: mostly muted — about 66% of the measured color is low-saturation (greys, dusty tones)
measured.caveat: Colors measured from Aesthetics Wiki images as photographed and displayed on screen; actual materials vary, and screen colors are approximate.
